title: How long? (Psalm 13)
hookLine: injustice cries out, and God hears the cry

lines: TWO WORDS AND A QUESTION MARK.
ON SIGNS AND IN WAITING ROOMS.
cards: Two words and a question mark. They're on protest signs and in hospital waiting rooms. A tenant says them about the landlord who won't fix the heat.
A family says them about a trial that keeps getting postponed. A child says them in the back seat, and a whole people says them across generations. How long?
It sounds like impatience. In the Bible it's something else: a prayer, and a cry about what is wrong. A short psalm asks it again and again, and the Bible keeps answering that the cry is heard.

teach.b: Back on day one hundred five, this psalm taught that complaint is a prayer too, and not long ago its first line came up as an argument with God.
Today, listen for verse two, where a third figure enters, the enemy: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?"
Someone is winning who shouldn't be. That turns how long from a sigh into a cry about injustice. And the Bible says that kind of cry is heard.
From the burning bush, God says in Exodus: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows."
Seen, heard, known, and every word points at people worked by taskmasters.
The prophet Habakkuk opens with the same complaint, about violence and judgment gone crooked: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!"

teach.h: HOW LONG, O LORD, HOLY AND TRUE?
teach.b: And in Revelation, the souls of those slain for the word of God cry from under the altar: "How long, O Lord, holy and true?" From the psalms to the last book, the question is never thrown out.
Then Psalm thirteen ends in a strange place. Nothing outside has changed yet.

teach.h: BUT I HAVE TRUSTED IN THY MERCY.
teach.b: But the voice says, "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." The cry and the trust come from the same mouth. How long is one of the ways people pray about what's wrong, and keep praying.

how: Christians pray the lament psalms, including Psalm 13, in worship and in private, and churches and Christian groups bring that cry into action through advocacy, legal aid, protest and care for people who are being wronged.

o: a prophet's question about when the temple would be rebuilt
a cry to God when wrong keeps winning, kept as a prayer

it speaks straight to God: how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?

in Psalm 13, in Habakkuk, and from the souls under the altar in Revelation.

games.q: you're the voice of Psalm 13. God seems to have forgotten you, and your enemy is winning. what do you do?
o: stay silent, because questioning God is not allowed.
ask God straight out, how long?, and then speak your trust.
give up on God and stop praying.
games.why: the psalm does both: it asks how long again and again, then says, but I have trusted in thy mercy. the question and the trust share one short psalm.

practice: Bring to mind one wrong that has gone on too long, far away or on your own street: someone underpaid, someone unheard, someone waiting for a hearing that never comes, and name it plainly.
If you pray, bring it to God in the psalm's own words, how long, O Lord; if you don't, just hold it in the open, without looking away.

wordCard.voice: How long? The cry of Psalm thirteen, spoken straight to God when wrong is winning, and kept in scripture as a prayer.

orig.note: Hebrew: until where? how long? — the words that open the cries of Psalm 13.

carryVoice: Your line: how long, o lord? In the Bible, that cry is heard, and kept. See you tomorrow.
